paragraphs: Training a scene with 3D Gaussian Splatting involves adjusting Gaussian parameters through a strongly nonlinear rendering process. This paper introduces an optimizer that uses curvature information to guide those adjustments while keeping computation and memory linear in the number of parameters. Its aim is to make second-order optimization practical for large scenes.

The method estimates only the diagonal of the Hessian using Hutchinson’s method, avoiding explicit or dense curvature matrices. It combines this approximation with a separate trust region for each parameter, based on squared Hellinger distance. These trust regions regularize Gaussian updates to support stable optimization despite the rendering process’s nonlinearity.

With identical initialization and no densification, the method achieves better reconstruction quality than ADAM using 50% fewer iterations on standard datasets. Reported peak GPU memory overhead is below 1GB: 17% above ADAM and 85% below 3DGS-LM. These findings support large-scene scalability; extension to distributed training is presented as a possibility.
icml-2026-3dgs-2-tr-scalable-second-orde.tldr: A matrix-free curvature approximation and parameter-wise trust regions improve 3D Gaussian Splatting training with linear computation and memory costs.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines scarce labels with unlabeled examples, but the unlabeled data may have an unknown distribution. The paper formalizes this setting as Universal Semi-supervised Learning. It argues that pseudo-labeling becomes unreliable when methods assume a uniform distribution or need more labeled examples than are available to estimate that distribution.

SAGE instead emphasizes relationships among learned representations, which the authors observe to be more reliable than individual pseudo-labels. It uses higher-order relationships among samples to establish structural agreement. A simplex equiangular tight frame supplies a geometric coordinate system that guides separation between classes, helping prevent their representations from becoming confused.

The method still uses pseudo-labels, but weights them with distribution-agnostic reliability measures and places potentially erroneous ones in an auxiliary branch. Thus, structural inference guides learning while the influence of questionable labels is managed separately. Across five standard benchmarks, SAGE consistently beats the compared state-of-the-art methods, with a reported average accuracy gain of 8.52%.
icml-2026-beyond-distribution-estimation.tldr: SAGE uses representation relationships and geometric class anchors to improve semi-supervised learning when unlabeled-data distributions are unknown.

paragraphs: A diffusion bridge describes a random evolving system conditioned on both its starting state and its ending state. Learning to simulate such paths is difficult when the desired endpoint is a rare event: the original, unconditioned process seldom reaches it. The paper addresses this problem by learning the conditioned dynamics directly.

Its central ingredient is a self-consistency property of the optimal control associated with the bridge. That property supplies the basis for losses used to learn the dynamics through repeated online updates. The resulting algorithm does not require differentiating through simulated trajectories, so its learning procedure avoids that particular computational requirement.

The authors report strong empirical performance across a range of settings, supporting self-consistency as a useful learning principle for diffusion bridges. They also connect the framework to recent work in stochastic optimal control. This broadens the conceptual contribution: the bridge algorithm is an instance of a control-based learning approach with links beyond endpoint-conditioned simulation.
icml-2026-control-consistency-losses-for.tldr: Control self-consistency provides an online method for learning diffusion bridges without differentiating through simulated trajectories.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate attributes so they can be predicted robustly. This paper examines hidden correlations: examples sharing one attribute value can contain underlying modes that are correlated with other attributes. Addressing only the visible attribute correlations can therefore leave an important part of the data structure unresolved.

CoDID jointly discovers these modes and encourages conditional independence based on them. This pairing is intended to retain mode information while separating attributes. However, the two operations depend on one another: mistakes in discovered modes can affect disentanglement, and the resulting representations can influence subsequent mode discovery. Naively alternating them can amplify errors.

The framework coordinates the two operations through meta-optimization to mitigate that amplification. Its architecture also changes as the number of discovered modes evolves, allowing the representation process to accommodate updated structure. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks. The contribution is therefore both discovering hidden structure and managing its interaction with disentanglement during learning.
icml-2026-coordinated-disentanglement-wi.tldr: CoDID coordinates hidden-mode discovery and attribute disentanglement to reduce error amplification during joint learning.

paragraphs: Group-based reinforcement learning aligns generative models by comparing samples within a group. This paper identifies a failure mode in which those samples rapidly become too similar. As within-group variance approaches zero, the differences needed to drive learning disappear, potentially causing unstable training, premature stagnation, or reward hacking.

Embedding-perturbed Exploration Preference Optimization, or E²PO, introduces structured perturbations at the embedding level within each sample group. The method is designed to maintain variance and preserve the discriminative signal throughout optimization. It addresses diversity inside the learning process, where the abstract reports that simply changing initial noise or increasing group size often brings instability or diminishing returns.

Experiments show significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art baselines and more faithful alignment with human preferences. The stated findings connect sustained exploration to better preference optimization for flow models. The central contribution is a mechanism for keeping group comparisons informative as training progresses, so optimization continues to receive a usable signal.
icml-2026-embedding-perturbed-exploratio.tldr: E²PO uses structured embedding perturbations to preserve within-group variation and improve preference alignment in flow models.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary grounding requires linking language to image regions under weak supervision. Whole-sentence embeddings can miss fine distinctions, while explicit token-level alignment can demand extra annotations or expensive cross-attention. ExpAlign addresses this tension with a multiple instance learning formulation that learns which language tokens and visual regions should contribute to alignment.

Its Expectation Alignment Head applies attention-based soft pooling to token-region similarities. This allows implicit selection of relevant tokens and instances without additional annotations. To stabilize learning across scales, the framework adds energy-based consistency regularization, combining a Top-K objective with multiple positive matches and a geometry-aware objective derived from constrained free-energy minimization.

Experiments show consistent gains in open-vocabulary detection and zero-shot instance segmentation, particularly for long-tail categories. On LVIS minival, ExpAlign achieves 36.2 AP_r, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods at comparable model scale. The authors also report lightweight, efficient inference, indicating that finer alignment need not require the heavy designs motivating the work.
icml-2026-expalign-expectation-guided-vi.tldr: ExpAlign learns fine-grained token-region alignment without extra annotations, improving open-vocabulary grounding while keeping inference lightweight.

paragraphs: A mobile interface agent can appear competent while choosing actions from memorized shortcuts instead of the displayed screen and user instructions. Faithful-Agent makes this distinction central to training. It aims to produce actions grounded in available evidence and consistent with the agent’s own reasoning, rather than measuring interaction ability alone.

Training has two stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches abstention when evidence is perturbed. Reinforcement fine-tuning then uses a guided advantage estimator built on GRPO. This estimator combines anchors with variance-adaptive tempering to prevent the learning signal from collapsing when sparse GUI rewards produce rollout groups with little variation.

A thought-action consistency reward further connects the agent’s reasoning to its behavior. The second-stage system raises the reported Trap SR from 13.88% for the baseline to 80.21%, while retaining robust general instruction-following performance. Together, the results support explicitly training faithfulness and preserving useful reinforcement signals when reward differences within groups are small.
icml-2026-faithful-mobile-gui-agents-wit.tldr: Faithful-Agent combines abstention training and a guided advantage estimator to improve evidence-grounded mobile GUI behavior.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often changes rewards during training through shaping, entropy regularization, or curricula. Such changes affect both the actor’s policy updates and the critic’s value estimates. This paper analyzes a single-timescale actor-critic algorithm when reward parameters may change at every step and samples follow Markovian dynamics.

Under standard assumptions, the authors derive finite-time bounds on both actor and critic errors. A convergence rate of O(1/√T) is achievable when reward parameters evolve sufficiently slowly, matching the best-known static-reward rate. The result also covers gradient-based reward updates with bounded gradients on the same timescale as the actor and critic.

The qualification on reward evolution is central: the theorem explains conditions under which changing rewards preserves the rate, rather than guaranteeing convergence for arbitrary changes. A separate analysis of distribution mismatch under Markovian sampling improves the best-known static-reward rate by a factor of log²T. Together, these results strengthen theoretical support for practical algorithms with evolving rewards.
icml-2026-finite-time-convergence-analys.tldr: Actor-critic learning can retain an O(1/√T) convergence rate when evolving rewards satisfy the paper’s assumptions and change sufficiently slowly.

paragraphs: Matching point sets by minimizing how far points move is sensitive to rotation. Gromov-Wasserstein matching instead minimizes distortions of their internal relationships, addressing that sensitivity. Its optimization problem is nevertheless non-convex and computationally demanding, making large point sets difficult to handle efficiently.

The paper identifies a broad class of distortion penalties that can be expressed as a simpler alignment problem in a lifted feature space. This reformulation leads to an iterative solver with linear memory requirements and quadratic time complexity, replacing cubic time complexity. The method is also differentiable and comes with theoretical guarantees.

The authors report processing hundreds of thousands of points in minutes. That scale makes the approach useful for geometric applications and for examining the optimization landscape itself. In particular, local minima of the GW energy encode symmetries of the matching problem. Faster computation therefore supports both practical matching and exploration of the geometric structure represented by different solutions.
icml-2026-gromov-wasserstein-at-scale-be.tldr: A lifted-feature reformulation enables differentiable Gromov-Wasserstein matching with linear memory and quadratic time complexity.

paragraphs: Hypergraph neural networks represent interactions involving groups of nodes, but obtaining node labels can be expensive. Active learning selects which nodes to annotate. The paper argues that adapting graph-based selection through clique expansion can distort this choice: rankings may become dominated by hyperedge size instead of informative group context.

HIAL is a training-free selection framework that treats annotation choice as influence maximization. It builds a weighted pairwise projection whose influence weights account for both hyperedge cardinality and feature consistency. This retains high-order context within a scalable linear diffusion process designed for homophilic hypergraphs, where connected entities tend to be similar.

The selection objective combines coverage in feature space with reachability through structure. Its monotone submodular form enables an efficient lazy greedy solver. Across eight benchmarks, HIAL consistently outperforms strong baselines in diverse homophilic domains. The results support making pairwise influence sensitive to group semantics when deciding which annotations will be useful.
icml-2026-hial-towards-semantics-aware-h.tldr: HIAL selects hypergraph nodes for labeling by combining context-aware influence, feature coverage, and structural reachability without training.

paragraphs: This paper studies what a softmax Transformer can compute through its prompt while its weights remain fixed. The central perspective treats prompts as specifications of computations and the Transformer as an interpreter. This gives a mathematical way to examine how in-context behavior can implement algorithms without updating model parameters.

The authors prove in-context universality through emulation: a fixed-weight Transformer can emulate computations supplied in its prompt and thereby approximate a broad class of continuous sequence-to-sequence functions. The result connects approximation ability to a mechanism for executing prompt-specified computations, rather than treating that ability as an isolated property.

They also establish composition theorems for one-pass and multi-pass execution. Prompts describing simpler subprograms allow the same fixed Transformer to execute their composition and assemble more complex programs in context. These are theoretical results about computational capability. They provide concrete mechanisms for understanding algorithm execution and composition in GPT-style models within the framework studied.
icml-2026-in-context-universal-approxima.tldr: The paper proves that fixed-weight softmax Transformers can emulate prompt-specified computations and compose simpler programs in context.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures statistical dependence between random variables, including high-dimensional ones. Neural estimators can measure it accurately, but typically require iterative optimization for each new dataset. InfoAtlas targets this repeated computational cost by learning a model that predicts mutual information directly from a dataset in one forward pass.

The model is pretrained on large-scale synthetic data containing varied dependence patterns. This training teaches it to recognize different relationships and map them to mutual-information estimates. A single unified model accommodates varying variable dimensions and sample sizes, allowing the same pretrained estimator to be applied across different dataset shapes.

Experiments show accuracy matching state-of-the-art neural estimators with a reported 100-fold speedup, alongside effective generalization to complex real-world settings. The practical change is moving the estimation workload into pretraining so each new dataset can be handled through inference. These findings support the approach as a foundation for dependency analysis where repeated optimization would be too costly.
icml-2026-infoatlas-a-foundation-model-f.tldr: InfoAtlas predicts mutual information in one forward pass, matching leading neural estimators’ accuracy with a reported 100-fold speedup.

paragraphs: Branching policies are important to the speed of mixed integer linear programming solvers. Their design traditionally relies on human-written heuristics. Learning-based alternatives can automate the task, but often depend on expensive expert demonstrations or optimize a training objective that does not directly reflect the solver’s overall performance.

LLM4Branch represents a discovered policy as an executable program with two parts: an LLM-generated program skeleton and a tunable parameter vector. A zeroth-order optimization method adjusts the parameters using end-to-end solver performance on a few instances. This brings feedback from the actual solving process into policy discovery without requiring derivatives of that performance.

The framework combines language-model program generation with performance-driven numerical tuning. On standard MILP benchmarks, the authors report a new state of the art among CPU-based methods and performance competitive with advanced GPU-based models. These results suggest that executable policies optimized against solver outcomes can be an effective route to automated branching design.
icml-2026-llm4branch-large-language-mode.tldr: LLM4Branch generates executable branching policies and tunes their parameters using end-to-end solver performance.

paragraphs: High-dimensional time series can mix meaningful dynamics with distracting variation. The paper develops the Recognition-Parametrized Gaussian State-Space Model to recover the systematic, potentially controllable state underlying those observations. It addresses difficulties separating distractors in generative and autoregressive models, alongside the challenge of learning accurate dynamics with contrastive methods.

RP-GSSM uses a neural encoder without a parametrized decoder. Removing explicit generative parameters directs representational capacity toward dynamically relevant state, while a probabilistic formulation permits maximum-likelihood learning without auxiliary objectives or ad-hoc regularization. Exact inference under a jointly Gaussian prior combines with the encoder to represent a broad class of intrinsically nonlinear systems.

The authors prove linear identifiability of the parameters in the infinite-data limit, leaving that guarantee explicitly tied to its asymptotic setting. In experiments, the model recovers physically meaningful states from noisy video more faithfully than competing methods, identifies controllable nonlinear dynamics more reliably, and shows substantially greater robustness to visual distractors.
icml-2026-maximum-likelihood-learning-of.tldr: RP-GSSM learns probabilistic latent dynamics without a decoder, improving recovery of meaningful state amid visual distractions.

paragraphs: Learning molecular properties from three-dimensional structures is constrained by scarce labels. Self-supervised pretraining can help, but the paper argues that methods adapted from vision and language often neglect molecular physics. It highlights a physical connection: denoising pretraining can be formally related to learning molecular force fields.

MOES-Pred focuses on how noise is introduced during that pretraining. Applying uniform noise indiscriminately across molecules can systematically bias the modeled molecular distribution. An energy sentinel mechanism instead adjusts perturbations for each molecule, using chemical prior knowledge to make the noising process sensitive to the molecular system being represented.

The molecule-specific strategies improve coverage of sampled conformations and the fidelity of distribution modeling. Experiments report substantial gains over mainstream approaches in both force prediction and downstream quantum chemical property prediction. The findings support treating noise design as part of the physical modeling problem: perturbations that account for molecular differences can produce representations useful for multiple prediction tasks.
icml-2026-moes-pred-molecular-structural.tldr: MOES-Pred adapts denoising perturbations to individual molecules, improving force and quantum chemical property prediction.

paragraphs: Vision state space models process images as one-dimensional sequences, so the order in which pixels or features are visited shapes what spatial relationships they learn. The paper argues that fixed scan paths can break local adjacency, fragment object structure, and introduce directional preferences that make representations brittle under rotation.

PRIS-Mamba organizes images into concentric rings. Within each ring, it aggregates information without depending on element order; between rings, short radial state space models capture dependencies. This factorization preserves isotropy while retaining linear complexity. Partial channel filtering further improves efficiency by applying recurrent processing selectively to informative channels and sending others through a residual path.

On ImageNet-1K, the method improves accuracy, efficiency, and rotation robustness over prior vision state space models. The findings make scan order a central architectural consideration: how a two-dimensional image becomes a sequence affects the representation itself. The proposed ring-based organization demonstrates a way to address that choice while preserving efficient computation.
icml-2026-partial-ring-scan-revisiting-s.tldr: PRIS-Mamba uses concentric-ring processing to improve vision state space models’ accuracy, efficiency, and rotation robustness.

paragraphs: Proactive recommendation uses sequences of intermediate recommendations to guide preferences toward target items. Reinforcement learning can evaluate these paths through short-term acceptance and longer-term guidance. The paper identifies two problems with applying policy gradients directly: an incentive to lengthen paths and noisy credit assignment across individual recommendation steps.

The first problem arises when step rewards have a positive mean, making longer paths attractive independently of their quality. ProRL subtracts expected step rewards so path extension contributes zero expected gradient signal. The second problem comes from weighting every step by the entire path reward. Position-specific advantage estimation uses the reward decomposition to construct step-dependent baselines and reduce variance.

Together, these mechanisms aim the learning signal at path quality while correcting the identified length bias and variance problem. Across three real-world datasets, ProRL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art proactive recommender systems. The results show the value of adapting policy-gradient estimation to the structure of recommendation-path rewards.
icml-2026-prorl-effective-reinforcement-.tldr: ProRL corrects path-length bias and reduces gradient variance to improve reinforcement learning for proactive recommendation.

paragraphs: Recursive Monte-Carlo Tree Search revisits how an AlphaZero-style search assigns values to possible actions. Its procedure separates construction of the search tree from a recursive re-estimation of action values. Prior policies guide the initial tree generation, giving the algorithm the structure on which its subsequent value computation operates.

The re-estimation then works from the leaves toward the root. At each node, RMCTS uses a regularized optimal posterior policy from an existing formulation of tree search as regularized policy optimization. Values are therefore reconsidered using these policies throughout the tree, with results from deeper nodes feeding into the calculations closer to the root.

The authors find that RMCTS matches or exceeds the quality of AlphaZero’s MCTS-UCB while taking a tiny fraction of the time. The reported contribution is a more efficient search procedure built around recursive policy-based value re-estimation. This finding concerns the evaluated search quality and runtime, with the bottom-up recursion providing the algorithm’s distinguishing mechanism.
icml-2026-recursive-monte-carlo-tree-sea.tldr: RMCTS recursively re-estimates tree-search values using regularized posterior policies, matching or exceeding AlphaZero’s MCTS-UCB quality much faster.

paragraphs: Sampling methods can use history to discourage redundant revisits and reduce Monte Carlo variance. Storing that history as an empirical measure, however, becomes problematic in large discrete spaces or continuous domains. Score-Repellent Monte Carlo compresses trajectory history into a running average of score evaluations, requiring memory proportional to the score dimension.

This summary defines a changing surrogate target through an exponential score tilt. A parameter α controls repulsion strength. The framework wraps a base sampling kernel by running it against the current surrogate while updating history online, without requiring the surrogate’s normalizing constant. Memory remains O(d), independent of trajectory length.

The analysis establishes almost sure convergence and a joint central limit theorem. It also identifies regimes where asymptotic covariance decreases with repulsion strength at O(1/α); this benefit is conditional on those regimes. Experiments on continuous targets and discrete energy-based models show improved estimator variance and mode coverage with modest per-iteration overhead.
icml-2026-score-repellent-monte-carlo-to.tldr: SRMC summarizes sampling history in O(d) memory and uses score-based repulsion to improve variance and mode coverage.

paragraphs: This paper shows that a deployed vision-language model’s observable task behavior can reveal private details of its visual tokenizer. The recovered information includes image patch size and preprocessing configuration. The attack is black-box: the leakage comes from responses to visual inputs rather than access to the model’s internal implementation.

The underlying side channel arises when synthetic image boundaries align with the tokenizer’s hidden patch grid. Tokenization can erase boundary cues, producing periodic drops in task accuracy that expose the patch structure. The authors also use padding and consistency checks to distinguish dynamic-resolution from fixed-resolution preprocessing and identify the target resize resolution.

Across open-source Qwen-VL variants and proprietary GPT and Claude models, the method reliably recovers tokenizer-related parameters. The paper further demonstrates that this information supports preprocessing-aware transfer attacks and model-targeted adversarial manipulation. Its central finding is that seemingly hidden image-processing choices can leave a measurable behavioral signature with consequences for adversarial robustness.
icml-2026-steal-the-patch-size-adversari.tldr: Behavioral side channels reveal private visual-tokenizer settings and can enable more targeted adversarial manipulation of vision-language models.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models can waste capacity when different experts process similar tokens and learn redundant functions. This overlap also makes routing ambiguous. The paper proposes two auxiliary training losses that encourage specialization without changing the router or model architecture, making them applicable to existing expert-based systems.

The first loss discourages cosine similarity between experts’ SwiGLU activations on the same tokens, encouraging complementary functions within a layer. The second maximizes joint Top-k routing probabilities across neighboring layers, promoting coherent expert pathways through depth. It also reinforces the within-layer specialization, linking local differentiation with consistent routing across layers.

Both losses complement standard load balancing and work with shared-expert and vanilla Top-k architectures. The authors provide a drop-in Megatron-LM implementation. Experiments spanning pretraining, fine-tuning, and zero-shot benchmarks show consistent task improvements, stronger specialization, and lower-entropy routing. More stable expert pathways also translate into faster inference, connecting training-time specialization to deployment efficiency.
icml-2026-synergistic-intra-and-cross-la.tldr: Two architecture-preserving losses encourage complementary experts and coherent cross-layer routing, improving task performance and inference speed.

paragraphs: A Rashomon set contains multiple models with nearly optimal performance. This paper examines how having such a set changes trustworthiness, beyond the properties of any individual model. At the individual level, the authors find that sparse, interpretable models tend to protect privacy but are vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

Diversity across the set creates another option: when an attack compromises one model, a practitioner can switch to a different near-optimal model that remains accurate without retraining. The paper calls this reactive robustness. Yet revealing additional models also gives an attacker richer views of the training data, increasing information leakage.

The authors analyze this diversity-driven robustness–privacy trade-off both theoretically and empirically. They additionally show stability of Rashomon sets under small distribution shifts, allowing a previously computed set to remain valid without recomputation under such shifts. The findings make model multiplicity both a practical resource for responding to attacks and a source of privacy risk when models are disclosed.
icml-2026-the-double-edged-nature-of-the.tldr: Diverse near-optimal models support switching after attacks, but disclosing more of them increases training-data leakage.

paragraphs: The paper proposes Atom Theory to define fundamental representational units inside language models. Its atomic inner product captures non-Euclidean representation geometry, and ideal units must satisfy two criteria: faithfulness and stability. The authors also identify a pervasive representation shift and show that their metric corrects it.

Under these criteria, neither neurons nor commonly used features qualify as ideal atoms. Neurons are fully faithful but have only 0.5% stability; features reach 68.2% stability but 48.8% faithfulness. The paper proves identifiability under threshold-activated sparse autoencoders. Large-scale experiments find reliable identification only when autoencoder capacity matches the scale of the data.

Using that insight, the authors identify units across layers of Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B, and Llama3.1-8B with 99.9% faithfulness and 99.8% stability, statistically satisfying their ideal-atom criteria. Further analysis finds substantially higher monosemanticity. These results validate the proposed units within the paper’s framework and provide a more faithful, stable basis for examining internal representations.
icml-2026-towards-atoms-of-large-languag.tldr: Atom Theory defines and identifies language-model representation units with near-perfect measured faithfulness and stability.

paragraphs: Image-editing models increasingly infer instructions from visual prompts such as marks and arrows. This paper examines the resulting safety problem: visual inputs can carry malicious intent as well as legitimate editing guidance. It introduces Vision-Centric Jailbreak Attack, which communicates malicious instructions through visual inputs, and IESBench for evaluating image-editing safety.

On that benchmark, the attack compromises leading commercial systems, with reported success rates reaching 80.9% on Nano Banana Pro and 70.1% on GPT-Image-1.5. These results demonstrate that the visual instruction channel can expose vulnerabilities even when the model’s task is image editing rather than conventional text-based interaction.

The paper also proposes a training-free defense based on introspective multimodal reasoning. It substantially improves poorly aligned models to safety levels comparable with commercial systems, without auxiliary guard models and with negligible computational overhead. The combined contribution is an identified attack surface, a benchmark for studying it, and an evaluated defense addressing visual interpretation within the editing process.
icml-2026-when-the-prompt-becomes-visual.tldr: Visual prompts can jailbreak image-editing models, while a training-free introspective reasoning defense improves safety in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Time series captions can make temporal behavior easier to interpret, but producing training captions often requires specialized domain knowledge. This paper introduces Caption Label-Free Learning to learn captioning without those annotations. It treats caption generation as exploration guided by a proxy reward, replacing direct imitation of human-written captions with feedback.

The Dual Loop Agentic Captioning framework separates proposal and evaluation. In the inner loop, a captioning agent reflectively explores possible semantic descriptions of the time series. In the outer loop, downstream reasoning evaluates those captions and produces a proxy reward, which feeds back into optimization of the captioning agent.

The empirical results support the sufficiency of this exploration-feedback mechanism for learning complex temporal semantics and generating captions without caption-label supervision in the evaluated setting. The authors also release TFTSC, an industrial expert-level time series caption dataset. Together, the framework and dataset advance the study of temporal explanations when high-quality textual training annotations are difficult to obtain.
icml-2026-words-towards-explainability-c.tldr: A dual-loop captioning agent learns time series descriptions from downstream reasoning feedback without caption-label supervision.
